876.title: Why Arjuna and Bhima fell
876.hook: Arjuna falls, then Bhima, who asks with his last breath why he is falling
876.carry: prasad: food offered first, then shared
876.tomorrow: will heaven let Yudhishthira bring the dog?
876.howItsDone: The falls of Arjuna and Bhima are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva. The Gita's teaching about food is lived in many Hindu homes: a portion is offered to God before the meal and received back as prasad, which is shared, and some families set aside the first roti for a cow or for someone in need.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the twins fell, Sahadeva for his pride in wisdom, Nakula in beauty. Your line was amanitva: keep the gift, drop the ranking.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `THE TWINS FALL.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, who threw his bow into the sea, is still walking. He's the one who heard the Gita in the chariot, who won Draupadi at her bridegroom-choice, who fought through the war. Then, on the high road, grief at his brothers' falling seems to catch up with him, and Arjuna falls too. Bhima, who has asked why each time, asks again. A little later Bhima the strong feels his own legs go, and lying on the ground, he calls out one more question, this time about himself.
screen: `ARJUNA STILL WALKING.` → `ARJUNA FALLS.` → `BHIMA ASKS ABOUT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: About Arjuna, Yudhishthira's answer in Ganguli's telling has two parts. Arjuna once vowed to destroy all their enemies in a single day, and he didn't. And he looked down on every other bowman. Yesterday's ranking, in an archer's shape. Then Bhima falls, and this time he asks about no one else: I'm falling too. Why? Yudhishthira answers him directly. You ate too much, you boasted of your strength, and when you ate, you never thought of what others needed. Then he walks on. Bhima's fault is the most ordinary of all: a plate. And Hindu teaching has a great deal to say about a plate. The Gita, the teaching Arjuna heard in the chariot, says the good eat what remains after an offering, and those who cook only for themselves eat sin. That's why, in so many Hindu homes, the first portion goes to God before anyone eats, often a small plate set before the shrine. What comes back is prasad, food made holy by being offered, and prasad is always shared: with the family, the guest, the neighbor. Many families set aside a first roti for a cow or a hungry person too. A meal eaten that way is the opposite of Bhima's. Bhima, who asked why every time, is the last brother to fall. Behind Yudhishthira now, only one follower is left: the dog.

segments.voice: Before your next meal or snack, pause before the first bite. Many Hindus offer the food first, with a quiet line or a small plate set before God, and then eat it as prasad. If you pray, try it that way today. If you don't, name in your head three people whose work put this food in front of you, and share one bite of it with someone. Bhima's fall was eating as if no one else were at the table.
Bhima. The second Pandava, the strong one, who asks why each traveler falls, and falls last himself before Yudhishthira walks on with only the dog.

877.title: Yudhishthira's dog
877.hook: at the top of the world, a god offers Yudhishthira heaven on one condition: leave the dog behind
877.carry: the divine in every creature, even a dog
877.tomorrow: what does Yudhishthira find when he reaches heaven?
877.howItsDone: The story of Yudhishthira and the dog comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva and is retold in recitations of the epic. The Gita's teaching that the wise see the same self in every creature is often quoted alongside it, and in Nepal the second day of Tihar, Kukur Tihar, honors dogs with garlands and a tilak.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna fell, then Bhima, for eating with no thought of others, and Yudhishthira walked on with only the dog. Your line was prasad, food offered first, then shared.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE THEY FALL.`

segments.voice: Two of them are left on the mountain: a king and a dog. Yudhishthira's brothers have fallen behind him. Draupadi has fallen. The dog that joined them at the start of the road is still at his heel. Then the sky fills with sound, and Indra, king of the gods, pulls up in a chariot. Climb in, he says. Heaven is waiting. This is the moment the whole road has led to. And in Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira's first answer is not yes. It's a question about who gets to come with him.
screen: `A KING AND A DOG.` → `INDRA'S CHARIOT ARRIVES.` → `"CLIMB IN."`

segments.voice: First he asks about his brothers and Draupadi; he won't go without them. Indra reassures him: they left their bodies on the way and are already in heaven. You, he says, will go up in yours. Then Yudhishthira says the dog has been devoted to him, and it should come too. Indra says no. You have won heaven and a state like a god's. Leave the dog; there is no cruelty in that. Heaven has no place for people with dogs. Notice how reasonable it sounds. It's only a dog, the offer is enormous, and no one else will speak for it. Yudhishthira refuses. Turning away one who is devoted to you, who is frightened and has nowhere else to go, he says, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it even for his own happiness. Then the dog changes. It is Dharma, the god of righteousness, Yudhishthira's own father, walking beside him in disguise. Dharma praises him and recalls an earlier test at a forest lake, when Yudhishthira chose to bring back Nakula, son of his father's other wife, out of fairness. Only then does he climb into the chariot. Now the twist. In the old purity rules a dog counted as unclean, and Indra's words echo that. Yet Dharma himself chose that shape. The Gita says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. One self, in the king and in the dog.
screen: `"NOT WITHOUT MY BROTHERS"` · `INDRA: LEAVE THE DOG` · `"I WILL NOT TURN IT AWAY"` · `THE DOG IS DHARMA` · then, large: `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY CREATURE`

segments.voice: Find one living creature near you: a pet, a bird outside the window, a person across the room. For a minute, just look at it, without naming it useful or annoying, clean or dirty. As you breathe, think: the same life that's in me is in this one. If you pray, you can see the Lord there; if not, simply see the creature.
Dharma. The god of righteousness, who walked beside Yudhishthira the whole way as a dog, and revealed himself only at the gate of heaven.

878.title: Yudhishthira in hell
878.hook: Yudhishthira reaches heaven, finds his old enemy enthroned there, and goes looking for his family
878.carry: heaven and hell are stops, not the end
878.tomorrow: why would God need to be born at all?
878.howItsDone: The Svargarohana Parva is the last book of the Mahabharata, heard in recitations of the full epic. Its ending reflects a common Hindu belief: svarga and naraka are temporary, places karma passes through, and the final goal is moksha, freedom from the cycle of rebirth.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dog at heaven's gate turned out to be Dharma, and Yudhishthira had refused to leave it. Your line was the divine in every creature, even a dog.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA'S DOG.` · `THE DOG IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: The chariot sets him down in heaven, and the first face Yudhishthira sees is Duryodhana's. The cousin behind the rigged game of dice. The man who had Draupadi dragged into the hall. The one who would not make peace. He sits in splendor, honored among the gods. Yudhishthira's brothers are nowhere. Draupadi is nowhere. Karna is nowhere. And the man who refused heaven's chariot rather than abandon a dog says, in effect, that he does not want this heaven. Take me to my brothers. Wherever they are, that's where I want to be.
screen: `DURYODHANA, ENTHRONED.` → `NO BROTHERS. NO DRAUPADI.` → `"TAKE ME TO THEM."`

segments.voice: The sage Narada tries to calm him: old quarrels end here, and Duryodhana died fighting as a warrior. Yudhishthira won't be calmed. So the gods send a messenger to guide him to his family. The path turns dark and smells of decay. Thorns, burning things, a river that scalds. It is a hell. Yudhishthira turns to go back, and voices call out of the dark. Stay, they beg. While you stand here, a cool breeze blows and our pain eases. Who are you? Karna, they answer. Bhima. Arjuna. Nakula. Sahadeva. Dhrishtadyumna. Draupadi. Everyone he loved is in torment, while the man who caused the war sits on a throne. Yudhishthira is furious, at the gods and at dharma itself. Then he chooses: if his presence comforts them, he will stay in hell. And it ends. The gods appear, and the darkness lifts. It was an illusion, Indra explains; every king must glimpse hell, and Yudhishthira saw it for his own half-truth in the war, about Drona's son. He bathes in the heavenly Ganga and finds his family in their true forms. Now the teaching. In Hindu belief, svarga and naraka, heaven and hell, aren't forever. They're places karma passes through. Duryodhana's courage earned him heaven for a time; one half-truth earned Yudhishthira a glimpse of hell. The Gita says those who reach heaven by merit come back to earth when the merit runs out. The goal beyond both is moksha: freedom.
screen: `NARADA: OLD QUARRELS END HERE` · `VOICES IN THE DARK: "STAY"` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY IN HELL` · `THE ILLUSION LIFTS` · then, large: `HEAVEN AND HELL ARE STOPS; THE GOAL IS MOKSHA`

segments.voice: This is the end of a very long story, so give it a quiet minute. Think of one person who is going through a hard time right now. Send them a short message, nothing to fix, just that you're thinking of them. Yudhishthira couldn't end his family's pain; his being there was enough to cool the dark. If you pray, hold them in your prayer as you press send.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: heaven and hell are stops, not the end. Tomorrow a new book opens, with a wedding and a sword. That's the end of a very long road.

879.hook: a wedding, a brother with a sword, and the reason the Lord chooses to be born

879.howItsDone: The story of Krishna's birth is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana; Hindus hear it in recitations and festival retellings, especially around Janmashtami, the festival of Krishna's birth. The Gita's verses on why the Lord comes, age after age, are among its most often recited.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Mahabharata serial ended: Yudhishthira stood in the dark beside his family, and heaven and hell turned out to be stops, not the end. Today a new book opens, the Bhagavata Purana, and a new story: Krishna as a child.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY ENDS.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: The wedding is over and the music is still playing. Devaki, a princess of the Yadu clan, has just married Vasudeva. Her cousin Kamsa, a prince of Mathura, wants to honor her, so he takes the reins and drives the bridal chariot himself. Conches, drums, gifts of horses and elephants. A happy brother on a happy day. Then, the Bhagavata says, a voice speaks out of the sky, without a body, straight at the driver. Fool. The eighth child of the woman you are driving will kill you.
screen: `A WEDDING CHARIOT.` → `KAMSA HOLDS THE REINS.` → `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Kamsa grabs his cousin by the hair and draws his sword. The procession stops dead. Vasudeva doesn't fight. He talks, gently. Death comes to everyone who is born, he says, today or in a hundred years. Killing your own sister on her wedding day won't change that. Kamsa won't listen. So Vasudeva makes a terrible bargain to save her life right now: I'll bring you every son she bears. Kamsa knows Vasudeva keeps his word, and lowers the sword. And Vasudeva does keep it: when their first son is born, he carries the baby to Kamsa himself. Before long, Kamsa locks them both in a prison and begins to kill their children. So why is this eighth child coming at all? The Bhagavata opens the book a step earlier. The Earth, weighed down by cruel kings and their armies, takes the form of a cow and goes in tears to Brahma. Brahma takes the gods to the shore of the ocean of milk to pray, and in his meditation the Lord's answer comes: I will be born, in Vasudeva's house. Hindus call this avatara, a descent. In the Gita, Krishna says it himself: whenever dharma fails, I come, age after age, to protect the good. That's what Janmashtami celebrates. As many devotees put it, not a god who stays far away, but one who comes down into the mess, and whose story starts in a prison cell.
screen: `THE SWORD COMES OUT` · `"I'LL BRING YOU EVERY SON"` · `THE EARTH, IN TEARS, ASKS FOR HELP` · then, large: `AVATARA: GOD COMES DOWN WHEN DHARMA FALLS`

Keep the paper somewhere you'll see it.

segments.voice: In the prison, Kamsa kills Devaki's children as they are born. The Bhagavata doesn't linger there. When six have died, the text says, a seventh child begins to grow in her. And this time something is done in secret. The Lord, the Bhagavata says, calls on his own power of illusion, Yogamaya, and gives her a task. A child is in danger. Move him.
screen: `A PRISON IN MATHURA.` → `THE SEVENTH CHILD.` → `"MOVE HIM."`

segments.voice: Yogamaya draws the seventh child out of Devaki's womb and places him in the womb of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, living safely in Gokula, a village of cowherds across the river. In the prison, people say Devaki has miscarried. The Bhagavata names the child from that night: Sankarshana, the one who was drawn out. Later he is known as Balarama, Krishna's older brother, and the Lord himself calls him a part of Shesha, the serpent he rests on. Then the Lord enters Vasudeva's mind, and from there passes into Devaki, and she begins to shine. Kamsa sees her glowing and understands: this is the one. But he can't bring himself to kill a pregnant woman, so he waits, and the waiting turns into obsession. Sitting, lying down, eating, walking, the text says, Kamsa saw that child everywhere. Later the Bhagavata draws a startling lesson from this. Kamsa reached the Lord through fear, it says, others through hatred, the cowherd women through love. What counts is a mind fixed on him. Hindus call it smarana, remembering, and it's why a grandmother murmurs a name of God over the stove, in the car and in the checkout line: Kamsa's constant thought, chosen with love instead of fear. Meanwhile the gods come to the cell to sing to the child inside Devaki. Do not be afraid, mother, they tell her. The one you carry has come to protect the world.

881.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Krishna's birth at Janmashtami. In many homes and temples devotees keep watch until midnight, the hour the Bhagavata gives for the birth, then bathe and dress an image of the infant Krishna and rock him in a small cradle with songs. Some families keep a Bal Gopal (often called Laddu Gopal) at home all year and care for him as a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the birth: Balarama moved in secret to Rohini, and Kamsa thinking of the child day and night. Smarana: keep the Lord in mind, always.
screen: `SANKARSHANA, DRAWN OUT.` · `THE GODS SING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata sets the scene slowly, as if it doesn't want to rush the night. The sky is clear. The rivers run clean. Lotuses open on the lakes, birds and bees fill the woods with sound, and a cool, fragrant breeze moves. The sacred fires of the brahmanas burn bright and steady. And in the middle of the night, in deep darkness, inside a locked cell in Mathura, the text says, the Lord appears from Devaki the way the full moon rises in the east.
screen: `A CLEAR SKY, CLEAN RIVERS.` → `MIDNIGHT, DEEP DARKNESS.` → `LIKE THE FULL MOON RISING.`

segments.voice: Vasudeva looks at the newborn, and it is not an ordinary baby. The child has four arms, holding a conch, a mace, a discus and a lotus. A jewel shines at his throat. He wears yellow silk. Vasudeva knows exactly who this is, and folds his hands in praise. Then Devaki speaks. Her praise is lovely, and then it turns very practical, very much a mother's. Please, hide this form. Kamsa must not know you were born here. And this shape is too much for ordinary eyes. The Lord answers with a secret. He has been their child before, in two earlier lives, after they spent long years asking for a son like him. Now this is the third time. Think of me as your son, he tells them, and love me, and you will reach me. Then, while they watch, he does what his mother asked. The four arms, the jewel, the radiance: gone. On the prison floor lies a newborn, like any other. That is the heart of the birth. The Lord of the universe makes himself small enough to be held. Hindus have a name for loving God this way: vatsalya, a parent's tender love. And they practice it. At Janmashtami many families stay up until midnight, then bathe a small image of baby Krishna, dress him, and rock him in a tiny cradle. Some homes keep the child Krishna, Bal Gopal, all year: woken, fed and put to bed like one of the family.
screen: `FOUR ARMS, CONCH AND DISCUS` · `DEVAKI: PLEASE, HIDE THIS FORM` · `"I HAVE BEEN YOUR CHILD BEFORE"` · `HE BECOMES AN ORDINARY BABY` · then, large: `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD AS YOUR CHILD`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, one cupped inside the other, as if you were holding something small and new. Let your breath slow into that shape. Devaki asked the Lord to become small enough to hold, and many Hindus picture baby Krishna in their hands just like this. If you pray, hold him there for a minute. If you don't, hold in mind someone small you love, and keep them there gently.

Seva, service offered to God, is lived in temple and festival work: cleaning, cooking, serving food and carrying the deity in procession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth itself: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby. Your line was vatsalya: loving God as your own child.
screen: `MIDNIGHT IN THE PRISON.` · `HE BECOMES SMALL.`

segments.voice: The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. Prompted by the Lord himself, the Bhagavata says, Vasudeva picks up his son, and the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river.
screen: `A NEWBORN SON.` → `THE GUARDS SLEEP.` → `THE DOORS OPEN BY THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, at night, in the rain. Then the Bhagavata adds Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests follows behind Vasudeva and spreads his hoods over father and child like an umbrella. Think about who Shesha is. In the ocean of milk, he is the Lord's bed. On this road, he's the Lord's umbrella. And the seventh child, drawn from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, Balarama, is a part of Shesha too, born to be the Lord's older brother; in many tellings of the Ramayana he came before as Lakshmana, Rama's brother. Bed, umbrella, brother: devotees read it this way, whatever the Lord needs, Shesha becomes. Hindus call that seva, service offered to God, and count it as worship in itself. It's why devotees are glad to sweep the temple floor, cook for a festival, or carry the deity in a procession. Then the river. The Yamuna is swollen and fast, full of waves and whirlpools, and it makes way, the text says, as the ocean once gave way for Rama on his road to Lanka. Later retellings add a basket on Vasudeva's head and the river rising to touch the child's feet; the Bhagavata's own account is shorter. A father, a child, a river giving way, and a serpent holding off the rain.
